files.lesson.md: --- order: 9 unit: using node: AC9M8A02 n2 uses: [AC9M7A05 n3, AC9M7N07 n2, AC9M8N04 n1] # each side drawn as a line from its rule assumes: [AC9M8A02 n1] # graphing y = mx + c is taught in Plotting a rule and Lines and their rules; graphing inequalities is class work title: Solving equations with graphs summary: Draw each side of an equation as a line. Where the lines meet, both sides are equal, so the x there is the solution. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A graph can solve an equation you have no method for yet: draw both sides and look where they meet. Calculators, spreadsheets and engineers do exactly this." app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8137 url: http://127.0.0.1:8137/index.html readySelector: "#sl-k" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: graph.yml#pic-solve, caption: "$y = 2x + 3$ meets $y = 11$ at $(4, 11)$, so $2x + 3 = 11$ when $x = 4$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@graph.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "The solution is the x where the two lines meet" say: "The solution is the x where the two lines meet." clip: - caption: { text: "2x + 3 = 11: draw y = 2x + 3 and y = 11.", say: "To solve two x plus three equals eleven, draw both sides as lines." } - caption: { text: "They meet at x = 4.", say: "They meet where x is four, so the solution is x equals four." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Change the right side to 7: the meeting point moves to x = 2.", say: "Change the right side to seven, and the lines meet where x is two." } - click: Make k smaller - click: Make k smaller - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "2x + 3 = 1: they meet left of the y-axis, so x = −1.", say: "For two x plus three equals one, they meet at x equals negative one." } - click: Make k smaller - click: Make k smaller - click: Make k smaller - expect: { selector: "#board", contains: "x = −1" } - wait: 1200 connection: plans-cross --- An equation such as $2x + 3 = 11$ says two things are equal. Each side can be drawn as a line: $y = 2x + 3$, and $y = 11$ (a flat line, because 11 does not change with $x$). In the Equations unit you solved equations with a balance and by backtracking. Now you solve them by looking at a graph. ## Predict: where they meet ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to which number the meeting point gives (x or y) is the whole lesson: students who read y here will read y on every graph." check: type: predict q: "The lines $y = 2x + 3$ and $y = 11$ are drawn. What is $x$ at the point where they meet?" options: ["$x = 4$", "$x = 11$", "$x = 8$", "$x = 3$"] actual: "x = 4. Where they meet, both lines have the same y, so 2x + 3 = 11. That happens when x = 4 (2 × 4 + 3 = 11). The point is (4, 11): 11 is its y, not its x." ``` $$2x + 3 = 11$$ On the line $y = 11$, every point has $y = 11$. On $y = 2x + 3$, $y$ is 11 at just one value of $x$. ## Run: find the meeting point ```step stage: run insight: "Dragging P onto both lines at once makes 'where they meet' physical: there is exactly one such point, and its x makes both sides equal." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag $P$ to the point where the two lines meet.", when: "P on y = 2x + 3 and P on y = 11" } ``` Drag $P$ until it is on both lines. Read its coordinates under the board. Which number is the solution of $2x + 3 = 11$? ## Investigate: reading the solution ```step stage: investigate insight: "The solution is the x of the meeting point, never its y; and a graph's answer is still checked by substitution." tasks: - picture: { ref: graph.yml#pic-solve, caption: "The lines meet at $(4, 11)$. The solution is the $x$: $x = 4$." } check: type: answer q: "On a graph, $y = 3x - 2$ meets $y = 7$ at $(3, 7)$. What is the solution of $3x - 2 = 7$?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["7", "7 is the y of the meeting point: it is the value of both sides. The solution is the value of x."] explain: "x = 3. Check: 3 × 3 − 2 = 7." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#kai" text: "Kai solves an equation with a graph. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: cross-read-y explain: "Line 4: 9 is the y of the meeting point, the value of both sides. The solution is the x: x = 4. Check: 4 + 5 = 9 and 2 × 4 + 1 = 9." - check: type: question q: "The lines $y = x + 5$ and $y = 2x + 1$ meet at $(4, 9)$. Which equation has the solution $x = 4$?" options: ["$x + 5 = 2x + 1$", "$x + 5 = 4$", "$2x + 1 = 4$"] answer: 0 explain: "The meeting point is where the two sides are equal, so it solves x + 5 = 2x + 1. Check: 4 + 5 = 9 and 2 × 4 + 1 = 9." ``` ### Solving with a graph Here is the method, one line at a time. ```worked 2x + 3 = 11 :: Solve this equation with a graph. y = 2x + 3, \quad y = 11 :: Draw each side as a line. (4, 11) :: Find where they meet. There, both sides have the same value, 11. x = 4 :: The solution is the $x$ of the meeting point, not the $y$. 2(4) + 3 = 11 \; \checkmark :: Check by substitution in the first equation. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Kai's working one line at a time. Which number did he take from the point? ### Which equation? The meeting point solves the equation that sets the two rules equal. ## Modify: change the equation ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a subtraction, a negative solution, x on both sides, an answer between the grid lines, and two lines that never meet (no solution)." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#subtract", height: 560 } tasks: - starter: "graph.yml#subtract" check: { type: board, text: "Solve $3x - 4 = 8$: drag $P$ to where the lines meet.", when: "P on y = 3x - 4 and P on y = 8", explain: "They meet at (4, 8), so x = 4. Check: 3 × 4 − 4 = 8." } - starter: "graph.yml#negative" hint: "The lines meet to the left of the y-axis." check: { type: board, text: "Solve $2x + 3 = 1$: drag $P$ to where the lines meet.", when: "P on y = 2x + 3 and P on y = 1", explain: "They meet at (−1, 1), so x = −1. Check: 2 × (−1) + 3 = 1." } - starter: "graph.yml#both" hint: "Both lines slope now. Follow them until they cross." check: { type: board, text: "Solve $x + 5 = 3x + 1$: drag $P$ to where the lines meet.", when: "P on y = x + 5 and P on y = 3x + 1", explain: "They meet at (2, 7), so x = 2. Check: 2 + 5 = 7 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7." } - starter: "graph.yml#half" hint: "P moves in halves on this board. The lines meet between two grid lines." check: { type: board, text: "Solve $2x + 1 = 6$: drag $P$ to where the lines meet.", when: "P on y = 2x + 1 and P on y = 6", explain: "They meet at (2.5, 6), so x = 2.5. Check: 2 × 2.5 + 1 = 6." } - starter: "graph.yml#never" check: type: question q: "Where do $y = 2x + 1$ and $y = 2x + 4$ meet?" options: - "At $(0, 1)$" - "Nowhere: they are parallel, so $2x + 1 = 2x + 4$ has no solution" - "At $x = 3$" answer: 1 explain: "Both have m = 2, so they are parallel and never meet: 2x + 1 is always 3 less than 2x + 4. The equation has no solution." ``` ### Subtraction Each task draws both sides of a new equation. Solve $3x - 4 = 8$. ### A negative answer Solve $2x + 3 = 1$. ### $x$ on both sides Solve $x + 5 = 3x + 1$. Now both sides are sloping lines. ### Between the lines Solve $2x + 1 = 6$. ### Never meeting $2x + 1 = 2x + 4$. Look at the two lines. What does the last lesson say about them? ## Practise: read the graph ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading the solution as the x of a meeting point, and naming the equation it solves, in mixed forms; the review keeps c fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A graph shows $y = 4x - 3$ meeting $y = 9$ at $(3, 9)$. Solve $4x - 3 = 9$." answer: "3" feedback: - ["9", "9 is the y of the meeting point. The solution is its x."] explain: "x = 3. Check: 4 × 3 − 3 = 9." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Two other lines meet at $(5, 12)$. Which number is the $x$?", answer: 5, explain: "A point is written (x, y): x first. The x is 5, and 12 is the y." } - check: type: answer q: "$y = 2x - 1$ and $y = -x + 5$ meet at $(2, 3)$. What value of $x$ makes $2x - 1 = -x + 5$ true?" answer: "2" feedback: - ["3", "3 is the y of the meeting point, the value of both sides. Which x gives it?"] explain: "x = 2. Check: 2 × 2 − 1 = 3 and −2 + 5 = 3." - check: type: question q: "The lines $y = 5$ and $y = x + 2$ meet. Which equation does the meeting point solve?" options: ["$x + 2 = 5$", "$x + 5 = 2$", "$x = 5$"] answer: 0 explain: "Set the two rules equal: x + 2 = 5. They meet at (3, 5), so x = 3." - check: type: answer q: "Review: where does $y = 3x - 4$ cross the $y$-axis? Give the value of $y$." answer: "-4" feedback: - ["3", "3 is m, the steepness. Put x = 0 into the rule."] explain: "−4: when x = 0, y = 3 × 0 − 4 = −4." ``` ### From a graph ### Both sides sloping ### Which equation? ### Review ## Make: an equation with a chosen answer ```step stage: make insight: "Building a second line through a chosen meeting point reverses the lesson: from the solution to the equation." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#make", height: 640 } hint: ["At x = 3, the line y = 2x + 1 is at 7. Your line must pass through (3, 7).", "Pick m first. Then find c so that 3m + c = 7."] check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ and $c$ so that the equation $2x + 1 = mx + c$ has the solution $x = 3$.", when: "3m + c = 7 and (m - 2)^2 > 0", explain: "Your line meets y = 2x + 1 at (3, 7), so 2x + 1 = mx + c is true when x = 3." } ``` Your line is $y = mx + c$. The green point shows where it meets $y = 2x + 1$. Move it so they meet at $x = 3$. (Your line cannot be $y = 2x + 1$ itself.) Stretch: write down your equation, then check $x = 3$ by substitution. ## Make: when do two plans cost the same, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "The solution is the x of the crossing, never its y; the paper task makes them pick which number answers the question." hint: ["Make a table for each plan at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 GB.", "Plot both lines on the same grid."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Two phone plans (made up for the task). Plan A costs 7 dollars a month plus 3 dollars a GB, so $A = 3x + 7$. Plan B costs 5 dollars a GB, then takes off a 9 dollar credit, so $B = 5x - 9$. On squared paper draw both lines for $x$ from 0 to 10 GB. At how many GB do the two plans cost the same?" steps: - ["Draw $y = 3x + 7$ and $y = 5x - 9$", "each plan is a line"] - ["The lines meet at $(8, 31)$", "at the meeting point both costs are equal"] - ["$x = 8$", "the solution is the $x$ of the meeting point"] - ["Check: $3(8) + 7 = 31$ and $5(8) - 9 = 31$", "substitute into both rules"] picks: - step: 3 q: "The lines meet at (8, 31). Which number answers 'how many GB cost the same?'" options: - "8, the x of the point" - "31, the y of the point" - "39, the two numbers added" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "31 is the cost where they meet. The question asks for the GB, which is x.", "Neither number is added to the other. Read x for the GB."] answer: "8" feedback: - ["31", "31 dollars is the cost of both plans at that point. The question asks how many GB, which is x."] - ["4", "Check: 3(4) + 7 = 19, but 5(4) − 9 = 11. They are not equal at 4."] criteria: - "I drew both lines on the same grid and marked where they meet." - "I read the solution from the x-axis, not the y." - "I checked 8 in both rules and got 31 each time." explain: "The lines meet at (8, 31), so x = 8 GB. Both plans cost 31 dollars there: 3 × 8 + 7 = 31 and 5 × 8 − 9 = 31." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. Choosing a phone plan is exactly this: two price lists, and the question of when they cost the same. Draw both lines and mark where they meet, then type your answer. **Also used in** - **Phone plans.** Comparing two price lists finds the usage where they cost the same, and which is cheaper either side of it. - **Business.** A break-even point is where the cost line and the income line meet. - **Meeting up.** Two people moving at steady speeds meet where their distance lines cross. ```teacher summary: Students solve linear equations by drawing each side as a line and reading the x where the lines meet, then check by substitution (AC9M8A02). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 15 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can solve an equation by drawing each side as a line and finding where they meet. - I can explain why the solution is the x of the meeting point, not the y. - I can check a graph's answer by substitution, and recognise parallel lines as no solution. struggle: Reading x, not y, at the meeting point. Ask 'what is the same about the lines here?' (the y), then 'which number goes into the equation?' (the x). before: > Do the Run and Modify boards yourself first. This lesson joins the two units: the Equations unit's equations (solved with the balance and backtracking) and this unit's lines. The key idea is which number to read. At the meeting point both sides have the same value (the y), and the solution is the x that gives it. Expect students to read the y: it is the most common mistake, and the Predict and Kai's working are built around it. The Make board uses two sliders and shows the meeting point in green. Any line through (3, 7) other than y = 2x + 1 works. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. 'x = 11' is the common wrong answer (reading the y). Do not correct it: the Run board settles it." - "Run: when P is on both lines, ask: what is the same about the two lines at this point? (The y.) So which number is the solution? (The x.)" - "Investigate: model the worked example live. Sketch the two lines, mark where they meet, then say 'the solution is the x, because that is the input that makes both sides equal'. Finish with the substitution check." - "Modify: the last task has parallel lines. Ask: what did the last lesson say about lines with the same m? Then: what does that mean for the equation?" - "Practise: for each answer, ask a student to say which number is the y and why it is not the answer." - "Make: collect two different lines that work and compare them: both pass through (3, 7)." - "Paper: the two phone plans are drawn on squared paper in books; the page marks x = 8 and that the answer is the x, not the 31. Books out, then check both rules at 8." stuck: - see: A student gives the y of the meeting point as the solution. ask: Put your answer into the equation. Is it true? fix: At the meeting point, read the x off the bottom axis. The y is the value of both sides there, not the answer. - see: A student cannot find where the lines meet on the negative task. ask: Which way do the lines get closer together? fix: Follow both lines to the left of the y-axis. The solution can be negative. - see: A student says parallel lines meet somewhere far away. ask: How far apart are they at x = 0? At x = 10? fix: "Work out both rules at a few values of x: the gap is always 3. They never meet, so there is no solution." - see: A student moves the Make sliders at random. ask: Where must your line go through? fix: Work out y = 2x + 1 at x = 3 (it is 7). Choose m, then find c so that 3m + c = 7. stretch: "Solve 3x − 2 = x + 5 with a graph: the answer is not a whole number. How accurate can a graph be? (x = 3.5)" support: Give squared paper and have students draw both lines from tables of values (x = 0 to 4) before using the board. leads: > Next: modelling with two lines. Two phone plans or two ways to pay become two rules; where their lines cross is where they cost the same. Where it leads in class: break-even points in business, when two runners meet, and solving equations that have no neat algebra method. exit: q: The lines y = 2x − 3 and y = 5 meet at (4, 5). Solve 2x − 3 = 5 and check your answer. a: "x = 4. Check: 2 × 4 − 3 = 5." explain: > An equation says two things are equal. Draw each side as a line: for $2x + 3 = 11$, draw $y = 2x + 3$ and $y = 11$. Where the lines **meet**, both sides have the same value. The **solution** is the $x$ of that point: here the lines meet at $(4, 11)$, so $x = 4$. The 11 is the value of both sides, not the answer. Check by substitution: $2 \times 4 + 3 = 11$. If the lines are parallel, they never meet, and the equation has no solution. ```

# Graph boards for "Solving equations with graphs". Each side of an equation is drawn as a line; P is dragged to
# where they meet, and its x is the solution.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -2, 14
plot: y = 2x + 3
plot: y = 11
point P: 1, 1, drag
# endregion

# region: pic-solve
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -2, 14
plot: y = 2x + 3
plot: y = 11
cross: 1, 2
# endregion

# region: subtract
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -6, 14
plot: y = 3x - 4
plot: y = 8
point P: 1, 1, drag
# endregion

# region: negative
widget: graph
x: -4, 4
y: -6, 10
plot: y = 2x + 3
plot: y = 1
point P: 2, -4, drag
# endregion

# region: both
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -2, 14
plot: y = x + 5
plot: y = 3x + 1
point P: 4, 1, drag
# endregion

# region: half
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -2, 10
snap: 0.5
plot: y = 2x + 1
plot: y = 6
point P: 1, 1, drag
# endregion

# region: never
widget: graph
x: -1, 5
y: -2, 14
plot: y = 2x + 1
plot: y = 2x + 4
# endregion

# region: make
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -6, 14
slider m: -3, 3, 0
slider c: -6, 12, 2
plot: y = 2x + 1
plot: y = mx + c
cross: 1, 2
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: graph
x: -2, 6
y: -2, 14
slider k: -1, 13, 11, 2
plot: y = 2x + 3
plot: y = k, dashed
cross: 1, 2
# endregion
